q: A driver drives at $72\,\text{km/h}$ and looks at their phone for $2.0\,\text{s}$. How far does the car travel while the driver is not looking at the road?
a: $72\,\text{km/h} = 20\,\text{m/s}$, so the car travels $20\,\text{m/s} \cdot 2.0\,\text{s} = 40\,\text{m}$. If danger appears during that time, the whole distance is added to the reaction distance before braking can begin.

q: A loose $10\,\text{kg}$ bag lies on the back seat. Why is it dangerous in a head-on collision?
a: When the car stops, nothing slows the bag down, so it keeps moving according to Newton's first law. It stops only when it hits the front seat or a passenger in a very short time. Its momentum is large, and the short stopping time makes the force many times the weight of the bag.

q: Why does the stopping distance not halve when the braking distance halves after the tyres are changed to ones with better grip?
a: Better tyres increase the deceleration and therefore shorten only the braking distance. The reaction distance $v_0\,t_\text{r}$ depends on the speed and the reaction time, not on the tyres, so it stays the same.
